lead: A packed absorber is sized, not guessed. Two numbers fix its height: H<sub>OG</sub>, the height of a transfer unit, says how deep the packing must be to move a fixed share of the solute; N<sub>OG</sub>, the number of transfer units, says how many such shares the separation needs. Their product gives the bed height. The method holds even when the equilibrium line curves, where a simple stage count would fail.
prereq: You need the Y–X operating and equilibrium lines from Chapter 3.2, the packing terms a, ε and Fp from Chapter 3.6, and the integral of dx/x from first-year mathematics.

blocks.text: Design splits into a height and a count. H<sub>OG</sub> is the depth of packing in which the gas gives up one unit of solute. It depends on the packing and the flows, not on the purity you want. N<sub>OG</sub> is how many of those units the job needs. It depends on the equilibrium line and on how far the outlet gas is pushed away from it.

blocks.where: Z is the packed height (m); H<sub>OG</sub> the height of an overall gas transfer unit (m); N<sub>OG</sub> the number of overall gas transfer units (dimensionless).

Y is the gas solute mole ratio, kmol solute per kmol inert gas, so Y = y/(1 − y); Y* is the gas mole ratio in equilibrium with the liquid at the same height. Limits run from Y<sub>out</sub> at the top to Y<sub>in</sub> at the bottom. The gap (Y − Y*) is the driving force.

G<sub>M</sub> is the inert-gas molar flux, kmol/(m²·s); K<sub>y</sub>a is the overall volumetric gas-phase coefficient, kmol/(m³·s·ΔY); H<sub>OG</sub> comes out in m. K<sub>y</sub>a lumps a coefficient and the interfacial area per m³ of bed into one measured number.

blocks.text: The mole ratio basis matters. Y removes the shrinking gas volume from the arithmetic, so G<sub>M</sub> stays constant up the column and the integral stays clean.

sections.h3: The integral, and the straight-line shortcut

blocks.text: For a curved equilibrium line, integrate N<sub>OG</sub> graphically: plot 1/(Y − Y*) against Y and count squares. For straight lines the integral has a closed form, because the driving force then falls exponentially from bottom to top.

items: Get X<sub>out</sub> from the solute balance over the column, using the chosen L/G.
Read Y* at the bottom from the equilibrium line at X<sub>out</sub>, and Y* at the top at X<sub>in</sub>.
Form the two end driving forces: ΔY<sub>1</sub> = Y<sub>in</sub> − Y*<sub>bottom</sub> and ΔY<sub>2</sub> = Y<sub>out</sub> − Y*<sub>top</sub>.
Take the log mean: ΔY<sub>lm</sub> = (ΔY<sub>1</sub> − ΔY<sub>2</sub>) / ln(ΔY<sub>1</sub>/ΔY<sub>2</sub>).
Divide the total change by it: N<sub>OG</sub> = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/ΔY<sub>lm</sub>.

blocks.text: H<sub>OG</sub> = H<sub>G</sub> + λH<sub>L</sub>,  λ = m G<sub>M</sub> / L<sub>M</sub>
blocks.where: H<sub>G</sub> = G<sub>M</sub>/(k<sub>y</sub>a) is the gas-film HTU (m); H<sub>L</sub> = L<sub>M</sub>/(k<sub>x</sub>a) is the liquid-film HTU (m); L<sub>M</sub> is the solvent molar flux, kmol/(m²·s); m = dY*/dX is the equilibrium-line slope. The two resistances add, the liquid one weighted by λ.

blocks.text: A liquid-side pair also exists: HOL = LM/(Kxa) with NOL = ∫dX/(X* − X), and Z = HOL × NOL. Use the pair whose coefficient you have. Note λ = 1/A, where A is the absorption factor of Chapter 3.5.

Plant engineers often quote packed height per theoretical stage: HETP = Z/N<sub>t</sub>, in m per stage, which lets a packed column be compared with a tray column. For straight lines, HETP = H<sub>OG</sub> × (λ ln λ)/(λ − 1); as λ → 1 the fraction tends to 1. A small HETP means good packing.

items: Collect the duty: gas flow, Yin, Yout, solvent, Xin, temperature and pressure. Fix L/G above the minimum of Chapter 3.3.
Choose the packing: nominal size, specific surface a, void fraction ε, packing factor F<sub>p</sub>.
Find the flooding gas rate from a generalized pressure drop chart using both flows and F<sub>p</sub>. Design at 50–70 % of it, away from loading.
Read K<sub>y</sub>a, or k<sub>y</sub>a and k<sub>x</sub>a, for that packing at those flows. Compute H<sub>OG</sub>.
Compute N<sub>OG</sub>: integrate if the equilibrium line curves, use the log mean if it is straight.
Multiply: Z = H<sub>OG</sub> × N<sub>OG</sub>. Add about 1.2 m for the distributor, sump and extra bed.

blocks.text: In an exam the flooding and K<sub>y</sub>a charts are given, not memorised. A factor of two on K<sub>y</sub>a halves the bed. Carry units at every step and round the built height upward to the next half metre.

figure.caption: The design sequence from raw data to a built height. The two middle boxes answer separate questions — how good the packing is, and how hard the separation is — and the last box shows where the spare 1.2 m enters.

spec.title: Packed absorber design sequence
spec.aria: Step-by-step design chart from gas and liquid data through packing choice and flooding velocity to the two transfer unit quantities and finally the packed height.

examples.question: A packed tower scrubs SO<sub>2</sub> from air with clean water. Inlet gas Y<sub>in</sub> = 0.0526 kmol SO<sub>2</sub>/kmol air, outlet Y<sub>out</sub> = 0.00503, inlet liquid X<sub>in</sub> = 0, and L/G = 2.72 on a mole-ratio basis. The equilibrium line is Y* = 2X. The inert-gas flux is G<sub>M</sub> = 0.015 kmol/(m²·s) and K<sub>y</sub>a = 0.05 kmol/(m³·s·ΔY). Find N<sub>OG</sub>, H<sub>OG</sub>, the bed height, the design height with 1.2 m added, and the HETP.
steps: Solute balance: X<sub>out</sub> = (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)/2.72 = (0.0526 − 0.00503)/2.72 = 0.01749 kmol SO<sub>2</sub>/kmol water.
Equilibrium at the bottom: Y*<sub>bottom</sub> = 2 × 0.01749 = 0.03498. At the top X<sub>in</sub> = 0, so Y*<sub>top</sub> = 0.
Design height 1.42 + 1.2 = 2.62 m; building height 3.0 m.
Check with HETP: λ = 2/2.72 = 0.7353, HETP = 0.30 × (0.7353 × ln 0.7353)/(0.7353 − 1) = 0.256 m, giving N<sub>t</sub> = 1.42/0.256 = 5.5 theoretical stages.
examples.answer: N<sub>OG</sub> = 4.74, H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.30 m, bed height 1.42 m, design height 2.62 m (build 3.0 m), HETP 0.256 m.
examples.check:
import math
Yin, Yout, Xin = 0.0526, 0.00503, 0.0
LG, m = 2.72, 2.0
GM, Kya = 0.015, 0.05
Xout = (Yin - Yout) / LG
dY_b = Yin - m * Xout
dY_t = Yout - m * Xin
dYlm = (dY_b - dY_t) / math.log(dY_b / dY_t)
NOG = (Yin - Yout) / dYlm
HOG = GM / Kya
Z = HOG * NOG
lam = m / LG
HETP = HOG * lam * math.log(lam) / (lam - 1)
Nt = Z / HETP
print(round(Xout, 5))
print(round(dY_b, 5))
print(round(dY_t, 5))
print(round(dYlm, 5))
print(round(NOG, 3))
print(round(HOG, 3))
print(round(Z, 3))
print(round(Z + 1.2, 3))
print(round(lam, 4))
print(round(HETP, 3))
print(round(Nt, 3))

traps: Putting mole fractions y into ∫dY/(Y − Y*) instead of mole ratios Y. That changes both the driving force and the integration variable, and gives a shorter, wrong bed.

Using the arithmetic mean of the end driving forces. For 0.01762 and 0.00503 it is 0.0113 against the correct 0.01004 — about 13 % too much driving force, so N<sub>OG</sub> reads 4.20 instead of 4.74.
Forgetting the 1.2 m distributor and sump allowance, or adding it before multiplying H<sub>OG</sub> by N<sub>OG</sub>.
Quoting H<sub>G</sub> as H<sub>OG</sub>. H<sub>OG</sub> = H<sub>G</sub> + λH<sub>L</sub> is larger than H<sub>G</sub> unless the liquid resistance is negligible.
Taking λ = mG/L and A = L/(mG) as the same number, or using total gas flow G instead of the inert flux G<sub>M</sub> in H<sub>OG</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the defining equation for H<sub>OG</sub> and give its unit.
quiz.a: H<sub>OG</sub> = G<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>y</sub>a), in metres. G<sub>M</sub> is in kmol/(m²·s), K<sub>y</sub>a in kmol/(m³·s·ΔY).

quiz.q: Write N<sub>OG</sub> as an integral and say what Y* means.
quiz.a: N<sub>OG</sub> = ∫dY/(Y − Y*) from Y<sub>out</sub> to Y<sub>in</sub>. Y* is the gas mole ratio in equilibrium with the liquid at that same height, read at the local X.

quiz.q: H<sub>OG</sub> is a gas-phase HTU, yet it contains a liquid-side term. Why?
quiz.a: The coefficient is overall, not gas-film. The liquid film resists transfer too, and its resistance appears as λH<sub>L</sub> = (mG<sub>M</sub>/L<sub>M</sub>)H<sub>L</sub>. For a sparingly soluble solute m is large, λ is large, and the liquid term dominates.

quiz.q: Why log mean instead of arithmetic mean of the end driving forces?
quiz.a: For straight equilibrium and operating lines the driving force decays exponentially with height, not linearly. The log mean is the correct average of that decay; the arithmetic mean is larger, so the column is undersized.

quiz.q: A packed absorber has H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.45 m and N<sub>OG</sub> = 6.2. Find the bed height and the design height with 1.5 m added.
For a straight equilibrium line, λ = 1.5 and H<sub>OG</sub> = 0.40 m. Find the HETP.
The example computes a 1.42 m bed but 3.0 m is built. Give two reasons the shorter bed could fail in service.
quiz.a: Part of the 1.2 m is distributor space and sump, and the real bed must also allow for maldistribution, which lowers the effective K<sub>y</sub>a below the chart value. Also, heat of absorption warms the solvent, raising the equilibrium line and shrinking the driving force, so more height is needed than the isothermal calculation says.

quiz.q: Gas flow is halved at constant liquid flow. K<sub>y</sub>a falls to 60 % of its old value and N<sub>OG</sub> stays the same. By what fraction does the bed height change?
quiz.a: H<sub>OG</sub> = G<sub>M</sub>/(K<sub>y</sub>a) scales as 0.5/0.6 = 0.833. With N<sub>OG</sub> fixed, Z falls to 83 % of its old value, a drop of about 17 %.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real columns are now checked with rate-based (non-equilibrium) models that integrate the Maxwell–Stefan fluxes point by point up the bed instead of trusting one lumped K<sub>y</sub>a. Vendors publish measured HTU and pressure drop data; structured packs reach much lower HETP than old random rings. CFD is used to study maldistribution and wall flow, where most full-size columns lose performance. Search terms: rate-based absorber model, structured packing HTU data, generalized pressure drop correlation, wall flow in packed beds.
